posts.name: Dalyodh Singh
posts.cooked:
I am not able to understand the real difference between 0 and 1 in bash script with this contradictory example.

I have declare only one variable starting with m as you can see in the image

Screenshot 2024-11-03 at 11.01.50 AM784×500 99 KB

CASE1:

[[ -z ${myvar+x} ]]
why echo $? gives 1 as it is already defined

CASE 2:

[[ -z ${myvr+x} ]]
why echo $? gives 0 as “myvr” is not defined,

look up output of echo ${!m*} for ref

0 indicated success
1 indicates failure

as suggested by @gphani
please @Puneet_21f3002005 @sayan

As confirmed by echo ${!m*} showing myvar, you’ve set the variable myvar to some value, say,

myvar="original value"

Let’s break down the command [[ -z ${myvar+x} ]] into 2 parts:

  1. [[ -z <variable> ]]: This returns 0 (success) if <variable> is an empty string.
  2. ${myvar+x}: This parameter expansion outputs x if myvar is set (even if it’s empty) and outputs nothing if myvar is unset.

So, if myvar="original value", then ${myvar+x} expands to x, making the command [[ -z "x" ]]. Since "x" is non-empty, [[ -z "x" ]] returns 1 (false). That’s why [[ -z ${myvar+x} ]] returns 1 when myvar is set.

Now, in your 2nd case with [[ -z ${myvar-x} ]], you use a - instead of +.
Here, ${myvar-x} returns the original value of myvar if it’s set; otherwise, it defaults to x. If myvar="original value", [[ -z ${myvar-x} ]] becomes [[ -z "original value" ]]. Since "original value" is non-empty, this also returns 1.

For [[ -z ${myvr-x} ]] (using myvr, which is unset), ${myvr-x} expands to x, making the command [[ -z "x" ]], which returns 1 since "x" is non-empty.

Lastly, with [[ -z ${myvr+x} ]] for myvr (unset), ${myvr+x} expands to nothing, so [[ -z "" ]] returns 0 (true), as the string is empty.

So, the confusion might have more to do with parameter expansion than what 0 and 1 mean in bash.

With respect to exit codes,

0 → No error
Positive value → Error

Hope this helps.

Thanks!

posts.name: Dalyodh Singh
posts.cooked:
you want to say that -z is checking whether variable is empty or not?
if it is empty, then return 0 as success.
otherwise return 1 as failure.
Yes, [[ -z ${myvar} ]] checks for zero-length. Returns 0 (true) when the string has length 0, otherwise returns 1 (false).
